clinicalPearls: A congenital condition defined by the imaging triad of a thin or absent (interrupted) pituitary stalk, an absent or hypoplastic anterior pituitary and an ectopic posterior pituitary bright spot
It is a leading cause of congenital hypopituitarism, ranging from isolated growth hormone deficiency to combined or panhypopituitarism
Neonatal presentation may include hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice and, in boys, micropenis and undescended testes; later features include short stature and delayed puberty
Posterior pituitary function is often preserved despite the ectopic location, so diabetes insipidus is uncommon
Diagnosis relies on dedicated pituitary MRI demonstrating the classic triad
Some cases follow breech delivery or perinatal injury while others are associated with mutations affecting pituitary development such as HESX1, LHX4, PROP1, SOX3 and OTX2
Anterior hormone deficits may evolve over time, so longitudinal endocrine monitoring is essential
Management is lifelong replacement of the deficient anterior pituitary hormones, including growth hormone, thyroxine, glucocorticoid and sex steroids as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome is a developmental disorder of the pituitary in which the infundibulum is thin or absent, the anterior pituitary is hypoplastic and the posterior pituitary is ectopically located at the median eminence, seen as a displaced neurohypophyseal bright spot on MRI. Interruption of the stalk disrupts delivery of hypothalamic releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary and the normal migration of neurohypophyseal tissue, producing variable anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. The aetiology is heterogeneous, with contributions from mutations in transcription factors governing pituitary organogenesis and from perinatal or traumatic mechanisms; because axonal antidiuretic hormone transport can terminate at the ectopic posterior lobe, vasopressin secretion is frequently spared.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of congenital combined pituitary hormone deficiency without the imaging triad
Septo-optic dysplasia and other midline developmental defects
Craniopharyngioma or another sellar mass causing acquired hypopituitarism
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
additionalInvestigations: Dedicated pituitary MRI to demonstrate a thin or absent stalk, anterior hypoplasia and an ectopic posterior bright spot
Baseline anterior pituitary hormone panel including IGF-1, free thyroxine and TSH, morning cortisol and ACTH, gonadotropins and prolactin
Dynamic pituitary stimulation testing such as growth hormone provocation and assessment of the cortisol response
Blood glucose monitoring in the neonate for hypoglycaemia
Assessment of posterior pituitary function, usually intact, if polyuria is present
Genetic testing for developmental transcription-factor mutations where indicated
redFlags: Neonatal hypoglycaemia and adrenal insufficiency, which are life-threatening if unrecognised
Evolving cortisol deficiency during intercurrent illness
Emergence of new hormone deficits over time, indicating progressive hypopituitarism
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and appropriate hormone replacement the prognosis is good, allowing normal growth and pubertal development; however deficiencies may progress, so lifelong endocrine surveillance is required, and unrecognised cortisol deficiency carries a risk of crisis.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal hypoglycaemia or prolonged jaundice to other causes and missing hypopituitarism
Assuming a single hormone deficiency is fixed, when deficits can evolve and require repeated assessment
Overlooking cortisol deficiency before starting growth hormone therapy, which can unmask adrenal insufficiency
Expecting diabetes insipidus and being falsely reassured by its absence
management: Recombinant growth hormone replacement to restore linear growth in growth hormone deficiency
Glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone for corticotroph deficiency, with sick-day dosing education and a steroid alert card
Induction and maintenance of puberty with sex-steroid replacement, and fertility support in adulthood
Prompt treatment of neonatal hypoglycaemia and vigilance for adrenal crisis
Lifelong periodic reassessment of all pituitary axes as deficiencies may evolve
Desmopressin only if posterior pituitary function fails and diabetes insipidus develops
Paediatric endocrinology-led care with genetic testing and counselling for developmental transcription-factor mutations
